Moscow is a renter-heavy town. Just 40.0 percent of homes are owner-occupied (2020 to 2024 figures), and the population estimate for July 1, 2025 is 26,721. Many sellers here are landlords or heirs rather than people who lived in the house for decades, because turnover runs high.

Housing measureMoscow
Population estimate, July 1, 202526,721
Households, 2020 to 202410,166
Owner-occupied housing rate40.0%
Median value of owner-occupied homes$376,400
Median gross rent$927

The median value covers every owner-occupied home in town, so your own house may land well above or below it. Houses near Paradise Creek, on the hillsides or toward the forest edge differ in condition and lot type from a 1950s house near downtown, and buyers price them differently. Downtown still has commercial buildings from the 1890s.

The University of Idaho gives Moscow a steady pool of renters and a calendar that favors certain months. The campus is the largest in the state, with more than 12,000 students enrolled and over 11,000 of them on the Moscow campus.

If your house has been rented to students, three practical points apply:

  • Leases often follow the academic year, so a sale that needs vacant possession is easiest to plan around a lease end date.
  • Rental wear is common. Floors, paint and kitchens may show it. A buyer planning to renovate cares less about that than one who needs to move in.
  • Tenants who stay through a sale keep their lease terms, so read the lease before you promise a closing date to anyone.

A cash buyer asks the same things a traditional buyer does: condition, lease status, title and the cost of repairs.

Moscow winters are cold and snowy and summers are dry. The roof, heating system and plumbing take most of the strain. A typical year brings about 50.9 inches of snow and 27.78 inches of total precipitation, with snow on the ground about 27 days. The January average low is about 22 degrees, and the record low is minus 42.

  • Check the roof for ice dam damage and worn flashing, especially on older houses.
  • Look at the furnace age and the attic insulation, since buyers ask about both.
  • Inspect exposed pipes and crawl spaces, where freeze damage tends to show first.

Snow cover on the roof and yard can hide problems from a buyer. If you cannot afford repairs before listing, an as-is cash sale lets the buyer price them in.

Moscow is in Latah County. The county treasurer mails a single bill in early November covering the full calendar year. Pay the whole bill or the first half by December 20. The second half is due June 20 of the following year.

Interest on a late second half is figured back to January 1, which the treasurer calls very costly. A postmark counts as the payment date, but the county suggests hand cancellation at the post office because the Postal Service no longer guarantees a postmark on all mail.

What to look for on the bill:

  • The parcel number, legal description, tax charges and any delinquencies.
  • A line labeled HO EXEMPT IMPRVMNT, which means the homeowner's exemption has been applied.
  • The split among taxing districts such as the school district, the city, highway and fire districts and the library.

Idaho's homeowner's exemption covers 50 percent of a home's value and up to one acre of land, up to a legal maximum that changes over time. The Latah County treasurer's tax bill page and the Idaho State Tax Commission homeowner page explain how to claim it.

The exemption belongs to the owner who lives in the house. When you sell, the buyer files for their own if they will occupy it.

Moscow School District 281 covers the entire city, with Moscow High School, Moscow Middle School and several elementary schools. Palouse Prairie Charter School and Moscow Charter School are also in town.

US 95 runs north to Coeur d'Alene and south to Lewiston and the Treasure Valley, and Idaho 8 runs east to Troy and west to Pullman. The Pullman Moscow Regional Airport is about four miles west. SMART, the Sustainable Moscow Area Transit Service, runs from the Moscow Intermodal Transit Center, and the Paradise Path gives walkers and cyclists an east to west route past the university and parks.

Residential sellers of one to four dwelling units must complete a property condition disclosure form. The rule starts at Idaho Code section 55-2501 and covers an individually owned unit in a larger structure too.

The form is where you describe material matters about physical condition, and the statute sets mandatory statements every form must carry. A leaking roof, a bad foundation or a failed septic system belongs on it. Idaho Code 55-2508 holds the standard form.

Selling to us does not change that duty. You still fill out the disclosure honestly. The difference is that an as-is cash sale means we do not ask you to fix what the form describes.

A cash sale skips showings, the buyer's loan approval and repair negotiation. A listing can reach more buyers and may bring a higher price. The better fit depends on your timeline and the condition of the house.

  • List if the house is in good shape and you can wait through showings and a lender's process.
  • Take a cash offer if the house needs work, the tenants are hard to move, or you need to close around a lease end or a family situation.

We base an offer on the house as it stands. We do not promise a price before we see the property, and you owe nothing if you decline.

To get a clear offer, have these ready:

  • The address and a rough list of repairs you know about.
  • Any lease, with the end date and monthly rent.
  • Your latest Latah County tax bill, so the parcel and any exemption can be confirmed.
  • Whether a mortgage or lien is on the title.

Once you accept, a title company closes the sale, pays off any mortgage or unpaid taxes from the proceeds and sends you the rest. Having the lease and tax bill on hand early keeps that process short.

Moscow is on the eastern edge of the Palouse in north central Idaho, close to the Washington line, and Main Street runs north and south through the middle of town. The city lies in a valley below the Palouse Range, in rolling wheat country on deep loess soil, with conifer forest a short drive east.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Moscow house while tenants live in it?
faqs.a: Yes. A sale does not end a lease, so the buyer takes the house subject to the tenants' rights. Read the lease for its end date and notice terms, and tell us about it up front so the offer reflects it.

faqs.q: When are Latah County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half or the full amount is due on or before December 20, and the second half is due on or before June 20. Interest on a late second half is calculated back to January 1.

faqs.q: Do I have to fix my Moscow house before selling it for cash?
faqs.a: No. We buy houses as-is, so repairs such as an old roof or worn floors do not have to be done first. You still complete Idaho's seller property condition disclosure form.

faqs.q: Why is homeownership low in Moscow?
faqs.a: Only 40.0 percent of homes are owner-occupied for 2020 to 2024. The University of Idaho and its large student renter population are the likely reason.

faqs.q: Does Moscow's winter affect when I should sell?
faqs.a: It can. The area averages about 50.9 inches of snow a year, and snow cover on the roof and yard can hide problems from a buyer. A cash offer does not depend on the season, because we inspect the house as it is.
